name: AI data centres
statements: b0
A massive heatwave swept across the United States in July 2026, straining the country's power grid and water supplies.
b1
Data centers account for roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percent of total daily United States water withdrawals.
b2
Texas county commissioners currently lack legal authority to impose restrictions on data center construction in unincorporated areas.
b3
The debate over AI data centers is a grassroots political movement that cuts across traditional party lines and demographic divisions.
b4
Secretive deals involving nondisclosure agreements between developers and elected officials have increased public distrust of data center projects.
b5
Communities that reject data center construction will experience economic decline relative to those that accept them.
b6
It is unfair for residents in unincorporated areas to lack regulatory protection against unwanted data center development.
b7
Local communities should have authority to make their own decisions about whether to permit data center construction.
b8
Texas Governor Greg Abbott called for a ban on building data centres in rural areas during a campaign stop.
b9
Approximately 30 data centers account for an estimated 57% of Quincy, Washington's property taxes.
Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction.
Data centers function as economic engines that revitalize struggling small towns through jobs and tax revenue.
Revenue from data center property taxes has enabled Quincy, Washington to fund extensive new public infrastructure and services.
No further significant legislative action on AI data center issues will occur in Congress until the post-election lame-duck session.
Communities have a right to restrict development that threatens local environmental and quality of life conditions.
States should increase county regulatory authority over data center projects in unincorporated areas.
Residents in Texas testified before state lawmakers expressing concerns about data centers being built near their properties.
Data centers account for 4 percent of U.S. power demand as of 2026.
The Ratepayer Protection Act creates a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when setting rules on large data centers' infrastructure costs.
The most common criticisms of data centers regarding water consumption, electricity use, and job displacement are often based on numbers presented without proper contextual analysis.
Blocking the construction of new AI data centers in the United States benefits China's position in the global AI race.
The number of local data center moratoriums will continue to increase as midterm elections approach.
Concerns about data centers consuming excessive water and electricity are legitimate and deserve serious consideration.
Texas should ban the construction of data centers in rural areas.
